claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 begins as a homogeneous high-temperature BCC phase with a nominally random solid-solution arrangement.
Intrinsic compositional fluctuations in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 drive the development of local chemical order during cooling or thermal exposure.
Local chemical ordering destabilizes the high-temperature BCC state.
Local ordering nuclei lower the effective free-energy barrier for transformation.
Lowering the transformation barrier causes secondary metastable or ordered phases, including FCC or B2, to nucleate within the BCC matrix.
Slow cooling or intermediate-temperature aging permits atomic rearrangements and development of local chemical order.
Very rapid quenching suppresses local ordering and freezes a metastable BCC state.
The proposed mechanism operates in a thermal regime that permits limited diffusion but not complete equilibration.
Differences in atomic size and bonding between Cr and Co, Fe, and Ni produce spatial compositional fluctuations in the nominally random alloy.
The compositional fluctuations promote nanoscale ordered regions that reduce local free energy.
Nanoscale ordered regions serve as templates for nucleation of FCC or B2-type phases.
Cooling rate and aging time govern the degree and spatial distribution of ordered regions.
Slowly cooled or moderately aged samples will exhibit more local chemical ordering than rapidly quenched samples.
Slowly cooled or moderately aged samples will contain a higher fraction of secondary phases than rapidly quenched samples.
A rapidly quenched Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 sample will retain a mostly uniform BCC structure with minimal local ordering.
Interstitial impurities can promote phase segregation during thermal aging.
High impurity levels may dominate transformation kinetics and make the local-ordering hypothesis inapplicable.
High-resolution TEM or atom-probe tomography can quantify the presence, size, and distribution of local chemical order in this alloy.
